title: A website that feels like her chair.
problem: The site had to do more than show good hair. A new client needs to know what to choose, what it may cost, and how to book.
kept: Rachel’s point of view, her work, and the Square setup that was already part of the business.
changed: We brought her work, service details, pricing, and booking into one clear site. The Hair Brief gives unsure visitors a place to start.
result: A new visitor can meet the stylist, see her work, and compare the options before choosing a booking or a conversation.
body: Hair By Rachel Charles is an independent studio in Phoenix. The work covers color, cuts, and extensions. Rachel puts hair health and a clear plan first. We built a site around that approach. It shows her work, explains the choices, and connects to Square.

A salon visit is personal. The opening pairs Rachel’s name with her portrait. Yellow and bold type give the studio a distinct look. Hair photos then show the work, rather than asking a stock image to sell it.

The useful choice is not always “book now.” Some visitors know the service; others only know their goal. Two clear actions serve both. Booking stays direct, while the Hair Brief leaves room for questions.

The booking page groups services by type. A visitor can compare the name, price, and description together. Color and extension work can start with a consultation. That keeps a complex service from looking like a quick purchase.

The Hair Brief asks about goals, history, upkeep, time, and budget. It suggests a place to start the conversation. Rachel still makes the hair plan with the client. The site supports that judgment instead of trying to replace it.
Square remains the booking tool, rather than a second calendar. The page moves from service to time to contact details. The service information helps people prepare before that final step.
Pricing, a first-visit guide, and the gallery each have a stable page. That gives Rachel specific links to share in a text. A client can find the same answers without searching old social posts.
The delivered site gives each visitor a sensible next step. Ready clients can book. Unsure clients can start a conversation. Both paths stay tied to Rachel’s work and way of working.

title: The film sets the mood. The website gives it a home.
problem: A film website must work for fans, press, and people in the film business. Each group needs a different piece of the story.
kept: The film’s artwork, dark tone, official credits, and the client’s own film material.
changed: We gave the trailer, press, credits, and photo archive clear places. Contact choices help each type of visitor start the right conversation.
result: Visitors have one official source for the film and a clear path to its trailer, press material, and premiere archive.
body: CC Films is a film company in Dallas. Its film Marrow needed one official home online. Fans need the trailer. Press needs facts and credits. Premiere guests want their photos. We built a site that serves each group without losing the film’s mood.

The poster already carries the film’s identity. We used it as the main visual, not a background to cover with effects. Dark tones, tall type, and fine rules support it. The trailer and premiere links sit beside the film summary.

A film site needs atmosphere and clear facts. We kept both by giving each section a plain name. Viewers can watch first. Press can find credits and source links. Neither group has to work through the other’s task.
The gallery has its own address. Its opening records the event, venue, and photo credit. A guest can return to that page after the premiere. The images are not buried inside a long news post.

The photo grid keeps the full set away from the homepage. That keeps the film’s opening focused. It also gives guests and collaborators one gallery link to share. The photographer’s credit remains part of the archive.

The trailer links to its official video source. Press references link to the original coverage. Film and company credits remain readable text. Those choices make specific facts easier to find and share.
The contact form asks why someone is writing. Press, film sales, joint work, and viewing questions have their own choices. The sender can name the task before writing the message.
The delivered site brings the film’s public material together. It gives viewers a trailer, press an official source, and premiere guests a photo archive. The work has a home beyond one event.

title: Show the craft. Make the first step clear.
problem: Painting and murals share craft, but they start with different questions. The website needed to show the difference without splitting the business in two.
kept: The studio’s identity, project work, local focus, and practical way of talking about a job.
changed: We separated painting and mural paths, brought project images forward, and placed the next inquiry beside the relevant work.
result: A visitor can see the type of work that fits their space, learn about the process, and choose the right project conversation.
body: Chromatic Painting & Design paints homes, shops, and murals. Its paint work serves Greater Phoenix. Mural jobs span Arizona. We built one site for both kinds of work. A paint job and a mural each get their own path.

The opening shows a painted building at full scale. That puts the studio’s work ahead of a list of services. Warm colors and clear type give the photos room. The images show the setting as well as the finish.

Painting and murals do not start with the same questions. We kept them under one brand, but gave them separate paths. A home repaint can focus on prep and access. A mural can begin with an idea, wall, and scale.
The paint page puts a finished home next to the service details. The quote link is easy to find. A second link leads to more work. Visitors can ask now or see more first.

The page explains prep, access, care for the space, and job stages. Those facts matter before a site visit. The mural path gives art its own space. It starts with the idea and the wall, not just the cost of paint.
Work examples link to the right service. Those pages lead to a call or a project request. The photos help a person choose the next step. They are more than a gallery to scroll past.
Paint work and mural work each have their own page. The studio can share the page that fits a lead. On a phone, the work and contact choices stay in the same order.
The site shows both sides of the studio: paint work and art. Visitors can see the work, learn the steps, and ask about the job they have in mind.

title: A place to start when help is hard to find.
problem: Someone looking for help may have little time or energy. The website needed a clear starting point and plain words for real situations.
kept: The goal of connecting people with resources, and separate paths for finding help and offering it.
changed: We organized the public site around needs and location. Clear labels, large choices, and nearby safety information guide the first steps.
result: People can start with a need or place, then look for a relevant resource. Those offering help have a separate path.
body: ClearHelp connects people with food, housing, and other resources. Someone seeking help may have little time, energy, or privacy. We built the public website around their situation and location. Finding help and offering help have separate starting points.

The opening offers a ZIP search and two large choices. Yellow, red, and blue separate their roles. Color helps with scanning, but every choice also has words. A person can begin without learning a set of symbols.

Many needs overlap. Food, housing, health, and safety cannot sit in isolated lists. The site uses plain situation labels and related categories. That lets a person follow the need, rather than guess an agency’s name.

The needs page offers both situation links and broad categories. Someone facing a crisis can start with familiar words. Someone planning ahead can browse the wider list. Both paths lead toward relevant resource information.
The listings show where help is offered and when it was last checked. A group may exist without having room today. Those details help people know what to ask before a trip or call.
The public search starts with a ZIP code and type of help. The site does not require an account to begin. The guides explain what help may include and what to bring.
A quick-exit control remains close to the page. Its warning says that leaving does not clear browser history. That limit stays visible. A safety control must explain what it can and cannot do.
The delivered public site makes the first step easier to understand. People can start with their situation, find a source, and check the next step. Volunteers and donors have a separate route.

title: Make the next question easier to ask.
problem: A first-time buyer and a property investor do not arrive with the same question. A single broad sales page cannot explain every next step well.
kept: The personal voice, client-supplied business facts, and direct contact with the lender.
changed: We organized the site by situation. Buyers, homeowners, investors, and realtors have distinct routes into relevant pages and tools.
result: Visitors can find the topic that fits, use public planning tools, and ask a more specific question without starting with one generic form.
body: Logan Loans explains home loans. Buyers, homeowners, investors, and realtors each have their own questions. We built a site with a path for each group. Guides and tools help people learn before they contact Logan.

The homepage pairs a house image with a direct introduction. Green and warm neutrals give the topic a calmer tone. The person and the home lead, not stock bank photos. Clear links keep the next step in view.

A simple opening cannot carry every mortgage detail. We used it to sort the starting question instead. The next page can then go deeper. This avoids asking a first-time buyer to read an investor’s path.

The tools page groups calculators and guides by task. A payment question and a refinance question get distinct choices. The page explains what each tool is for before opening it. A reader does not need to provide an email to browse.

Planning figures need context. The inputs and notes belong near the result. A tool can help someone ask a better question. It is not a loan offer. The lender still checks the facts and terms for each loan.
Each path connects to loan pages, tools, and guides. Contact remains a separate choice, not the price of reading. Visitors can take a specific question to Logan when ready.

The site gives the tools a shared home and stable links. That is useful when a realtor sends a buyer one page. Program facts and terms stay with the lender’s own pages instead of being copied into this case study.

The site breaks a broad loan topic into smaller tasks. Visitors can choose a path, explore the numbers, and ask a clear question. The site helps them prepare for the talk. Loan decisions stay with the lender.

title: The room has a point of view. So does the site.
problem: A venue website must show the feel of the place and answer practical questions. A visitor still needs the menu, location, and a way to check what is on.
kept: The venue’s name, real game-room photographs, supplied menu information, and direct phone and map contacts.
changed: We organized the site around playing, eating, and visiting. Bold type gives it character, while the menu and venue details stay easy to reach.
result: Visitors can explore the room, read the menu, and find directions or a phone number from one public website.
body: The Break Room is a pool hall in Glendale, Arizona. Pool, darts, food, and sports shape a visit. We built a site that puts the room and those choices together. It pairs bold artwork with room photos and useful visit details.
Large type gives the opening the feel of a venue poster. Blue links tie into the pool imagery. The menu action sits in the opening rather than being hidden behind the visual treatment.
The opening artwork is a campaign concept. Room photos appear in their own section and show the real space. The labels make the difference clear. A bold ad image is not a photo of a finished room.

The games section pairs a pool-table image with activity tabs. Pool, darts, foosball, and patios remain named choices. The image sets the scene while the labels help people explore what matters to their visit.
Food and drinks have readable menu sections. Directions and contact details sit in the visit section. A guest can check the basics without piecing together screenshots and social posts.
The same site connects game information, the menu, group details, and a map. Those links give visitors paths into a night out. The phone view keeps the practical choices close.
Current events need a maintained source. The site distinguishes a proposed lineup from a confirmed plan. Where a detail needs checking, a direct contact route is more useful than a made-up answer.
The site gives the venue one public home. It shows the room, explains the choices, and helps guests plan a visit. Labels keep the campaign art and real room photos distinct.

title: The neighborhood bar, before you walk in.
problem: A bar’s menu and plans can change. Guests need a clear source for current details, not a chain of old posts or a menu image that is hard to read.
kept: The bar’s identity, real photographs, supplied menu, and existing event and social destinations.
changed: We brought the menu, event information, gallery, and directions together. The menu also has its own route for people arriving through a QR code.
result: Guests can see the real bar, read the menu, explore events, and choose a map link before setting out.
body: Easy Tiger Bar is a neighborhood bar in Glendale, Arizona. Guests need the menu, events, and directions. The person running the bar also needs a practical way to update things. We built a guest site and a separate menu-and-poster editing flow.

The brief called for a neighborhood bar, not a nightclub ad. We used supplied photos of the room, drinks, and people. The menu pairs a readable list with bar photographs. A guest sees the place while choosing a drink.

One person needs to keep the content moving. The menu flow stays focused on cocktails and event posters. Stock counts and recipes do not sit in the routine editing path. That keeps a menu change from turning into an inventory task.

Menu names, notes, and prices are text. Categories organize the list, with photographs alongside it. A guest can read the choices on a phone without pinching an image. The same page has a direct link from the main navigation.

The QR code points to that maintained menu page. Its separate print-and-share page does not create a second menu. Updating the menu need not mean replacing the QR destination. The address stays useful after the first print run.

The editing flow separates a draft from publication. The owner can prepare menu changes before making them public. Event posters have a separate place, since not every in-house event needs a ticket listing.

The guest site still links to Eventbrite for listed events. Visit details offer both Google Maps and Apple Maps. These are distinct handoffs: a menu for guests, a calendar source for events, and a map for the trip.
The delivered work connects the public site with the bar’s upkeep needs. Guests get a readable menu and real photos. Menu drafts and poster tools give updates a defined path before publication.

title: A personal service with a clear first step.
problem: Someone new to tarot may not know what to ask. The site needed to explain each format and help them choose a first step.
kept: Rachel’s personal approach, the focus on a conversation, and the clear boundary that the visitor makes their own choices.
changed: We gave the reading formats clear descriptions and next steps. A first-reading guide and a question path help people who are not ready to choose.
result: Visitors can compare a voice note with a live talk. They can choose a next step without knowing tarot terms.
body: The Tarot Hotline is Rachel Hope’s reading service. Visitors may know their question but not which format fits. We built a site that explains the choices first. Voice notes, live talks, and a question-first path each have their own place.

The red rotary phone puts a clear image to the hotline name. It gives the homepage one strong visual idea. Cream type and a dark green ground keep the reading choices clear. The look creates a mood without hiding the service.

The key design choice is what to show first. A visitor sees the format, scope, and price before the next step. A voice note and a live talk are not the same service. The Ask Rachel option gives unsure visitors a way in.

The readings page puts each choice in its own card. The card explains how it works before the button. Visitors can choose a voice note or a live talk. Ask Rachel sits beside them, not in a hidden help page.

That free path matters for someone new to the service. A first-reading guide answers the basics. The site leaves room to learn how a reading works before choosing a paid format. A visitor can ask first.
Each card leads to the next step for that service. Forms, time choices, and Square payments each have a role. The service details come before that handoff. The visitor knows what they chose.

Terms, privacy notes, and first-reading guidance have their own pages. The details stay easy to find beyond the homepage. Rachel brings her own approach to a reading. The site gives it a clear structure.
The site gives a personal service a clear home. Visitors can meet Rachel, compare formats, and choose a next step. A reading leaves room to reflect. The visitor stays in charge of their own choices.
